purpose: explain a change and invite a response
prompt: Your free photography class has moved from the library to the community centre. Write to a classmate who missed the announcement. Explain where and when the next class will take place, say what participants should bring, and suggest travelling there together.

requiredPoints: Give the new place and time

successCriteria: The reader can act on every practical detail
The tone is friendly and direct
Events and plans are linked with clear time expressions
The message has an opening and a natural closing

purpose: evaluate a proposal and defend a position
prompt: A local council is considering an equipment library where residents could borrow tools, sports equipment, and kitchen machines. Discuss two likely benefits and one practical difficulty. Decide whether the council should fund a one-year trial and support your view with reasons or examples.

requiredPoints: Give a justified decision about the trial

successCriteria: Paragraphs each develop one main idea
Examples are relevant rather than decorative
Connectors show contrast, consequence, and qualification

prompt: Students report that the central library does not offer enough reliable quiet study space during busy periods. Write a proposal that identifies the main causes, recommends two feasible changes, and explains how the library could test whether those changes work over six weeks.

requiredPoints: Identify plausible causes without presenting guesses as facts
Define a six-week test and useful evidence

successCriteria: Headings make the proposal easy to scan
Recommendations follow logically from the stated causes
The evaluation method includes both use data and user feedback
The register is concise, constructive, and formal

audience: organisers of a civic learning programme
purpose: compare two fictional formats and make a conditional recommendation
prompt: A civic learning programme tested two public-dialogue formats. In ‘Open Table’, twelve residents discussed one question for ninety minutes with a facilitator. In ‘Question Trail’, visitors moved through five short stations, leaving written responses before a final twenty-minute conversation. Write a critical review of the two formats. Compare the depth and inclusiveness each might support, identify what evidence is still missing, and recommend when each format should be used.

requiredPoints: Separate known design facts from predictions

successCriteria: The review synthesises criteria instead of describing formats one after another
Evaluation uses precise and appropriately cautious language
Concessions and limitations sharpen the recommendation
The conclusion gives organisers a usable decision rule
Complex sentences remain controlled and readable
